a male given name from English, equivalent to English Stephen

1000372.etyen:
Borrowed from English Steven (“male given name”), a variant spelling of Stephen, from Latin Stephanus (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Στέφανος (Stéphanos, “male given name”), from Ancient Greek στέφανος (stéphanos, “wreath, crown”). First attested in 1820 in Norway.
Compare Danish Steven and Swedish Steven (“male given names”).

en.g: Switzerland; a country in Europe, located in Central Europe, with Bern as its capital
x: Hun flyttet til Sveits for å studere.
She moved to Switzerland to study.
Sveits. Så får vi ta med os Sveits til middag og holde en tale for det: Kollega, vort store mål er å likne dig.
Switzerland. Then we shall invite Switzerland to dinner and make a speech for it: Colleague, our great aim is to resemble you.

1000628.etyen:
Derived from German Schweiz (“Switzerland”), from German Schwyz, the name of one of the three original cantons of the Old Swiss Confederacy. The place name is first attested as Medieval Latin in Suuites in a document dated 924, possibly written around 960. Its further origin is uncertain; proposals connect it either with a root meaning “to shine, shimmer”, possibly referring to a body of water, or with a root meaning “to singe, burn”, possibly referring to a clearing or land cleared by burning.
Compare the parallel German-derived forms Danish Schweiz, Finnish Sveitsi, Latvian Šveice and Hungar

en.g: a town in Røros, Trøndelag, Norway, the administrative centre of the municipality and a historic bergstad (“mining town”)

1000884.etyen:
Originally a farm name. First attested in c. 1530 as Røraas; the name later passed to the mining town and municipality. From the river name Røa, whose mouth lies in Glåma by the old Røros farm, and os (“river mouth”), with the first element in a historical genitive or linking form; literally “Røa's river mouth”.
The river name Røa continues Old Norse *Røyðr, probably ultimately connected with Old Norse rauðr (“red”), though the precise motivation of the river name is uncertain.
Compare the second element with Norwegian Nynorsk os, Danish os, Swedish os, Icelandic ós and Faroese ósur (“river mo

1001396.etyen: Inherited from Danish gjennem, older spelling of gennem, from Old Norse gegnum, dative plural of gegn. The spelling in -om was influenced by Nynorsk. Gjennom and mellom (“between”) were introduced as byforms in Bokmål in 1917 and made the sole standard in 1938. Though rare up until that time, they established themselves quickly as they had little bearing on pronunciation and were etymologically more correct (compare stundom, which had always been spelt thus).
